title: The Postwar Threat to Gulf Energy Infrastructure
gist: CSIS's Byman and Ness argue that as Gulf states build Hormuz-bypass pipelines (Goldman sees ~4 mb/d of added export capacity by end-2027 and 7+ mb/d by end-2028), Iran and its proxies will shift to drone, missile and sabotage attacks on pipelines, pumping stations, processing hubs and terminals. Disruptions will likely be episodic, with Iraq most vulnerable but least likely to be targeted, and Western oil majors facing rising regional risk costs.

themes.theme: Hormuz war shock and bypass buildout

insights.claim: A month into the US-Israeli war against Iran, Saudi oil exports had fallen by more than a third, UAE exports by over 50 percent, Kuwait's and Iraq's had nearly ceased, and Qatar's and the UAE's LNG exports were entirely cut off.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the 2026 Gulf supply shock for oil and LNG markets.
insights.quote: A month into the war, Saudi Arabia’s oil exports had fallen by more than a third, those of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) were reduced by over 50 percent, and Kuwait’s and Iraq’s had ceased almost completely.
insights.locator: In the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran

insights.claim: At least seven new or expanded pipeline projects aim to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which Goldman Sachs estimates could add almost 4 million barrels per day of export capacity by end-2027 and over 7 million by end-2028.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Bypass capacity would reduce the Hormuz risk premium in oil over 2027-2028 and drive large midstream capex.
insights.quote: Goldman Sachs estimates that these projects could add almost 4 million barrels of export capacity per day by the end of 2027 and over 7 million by the end of 2028.
insights.locator: As the on-again, off-again conflict continues

insights.claim: Gulf national oil companies are adapting by self-insuring, relying on US government insurance, buying their own tankers and altering ship-to-ship operations.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Commercial marine insurers and tanker owners are being partly displaced by state-backed risk-bearing.
insights.locator: As the on-again, off-again conflict continues

insights.claim: Repairing and improving Gulf pipelines, refineries and other infrastructure will cost the Gulf states tens of billions of dollars or more.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Big reconstruction and hardening spend benefits oilfield services and EPC contractors.
insights.locator: From a security point of view

insights.claim: The authors expect Iran to target the new bypass pipelines and other infrastructure that diffuses Gulf export capacity, because that diffusion threatens Tehran's coercive leverage.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Bypass pipelines reduce but do not eliminate the geopolitical risk premium.

insights.claim: In July 2026, Iranian-backed Houthis began targeting Saudi tankers in the Bab el-Mandab, threatening the Red Sea route that bypass pipelines rely on.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Red Sea exports from Yanbu are not a safe haven, sustaining freight and insurance premia.

insights.claim: The authors judge Iranian disruptions will probably be episodic and incomplete, with exporters absorbing some as a cost of doing business in a back-and-forth of sabotage and repair.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Suggests recurring supply spikes rather than a sustained structural outage.
insights.quote: Any Iranian disruptions, however, will probably be episodic and incomplete.

insights.claim: Iranian-produced UAVs such as the Samad-3, starting at about $10,000 per unit, can reach almost all Gulf territory from western Iran, northern Yemen or southern Iraq and can overwhelm deployed air defenses in swarms.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cheap drones make defending dispersed energy assets cost-prohibitive, favoring low-cost counter-UAS vendors.
insights.quote: The cost of these drones begins at approximately $10,000 per unit.

insights.claim: An ACLED analysis found over 70 percent of strikes on critical infrastructure that penetrated air defenses during the 2026 war (through August) caused damage.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Leakage through Gulf air defenses is high, supporting persistent risk premia.

insights.claim: April 2026 UAV strikes on Saudi central processing facilities halted the Khurais and Manifa fields, cutting output by a combined 600,000 barrels per day.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shows processing nodes are high-leverage targets for supply disruption.

insights.claim: Missile attacks on Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG terminal in mid-2026 disabled high-capacity trains that will reportedly take until 2027 to fix, as gas and LNG facilities require longer repairs than oil facilities.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Prolonged Qatari LNG outage tightens global LNG markets into 2027.

insights.claim: Gulf oil systems are dominated by vertically integrated national oil companies with highly consolidated mega-facilities and little cross-border integration, so a single attack can trap output with no alternate route.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Concentration risk means single-node hits move global prices disproportionately.
insights.quote: When an attack limiting processing or export capacity takes place, extracted product is often trapped in a singular network with no way out.

insights.claim: The 2019 Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's Abqaiq plant took over 5 million barrels per day offline for about three weeks, a temporary 5 percent cut in global energy supply.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Benchmark for the market impact of a single successful strike.

insights.claim: Iraq is likely the most vulnerable Gulf exporter due to oil dependence, aging concentrated export infrastructure and Iran-aligned militias, but Iran has strategic reasons to avoid striking Iraqi state infrastructure since Baghdad is a de facto partner.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Kurdish and foreign-operated Iraqi assets bear more risk than federal Iraqi assets.
insights.quote: Iraq is probably the country most vulnerable to attacks on its oil and gas infrastructure, though Iran may hesitate to strike it.

insights.claim: Regional sources claim up to half of UAV attacks during the war came from groups in Iraq, including strikes on Saudi oil fields and a Yanbu refinery that prompted Saudi strikes on those militias.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Iraqi militias are a major vector of risk to Saudi Red Sea export infrastructure.
insights.locator: Iran-backed Shia Muslim groups in Iraq

insights.claim: Iran attacked the UAE more than any other country in the war, yet Reuters reported in June 2026 that the UAE agreed to make billions available to Iran in a de-escalation arrangement, which Abu Dhabi denied.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gulf states may hedge with payments to Tehran, signaling fragmented GCC posture.
insights.locator: However, the Gulf countries are not a unified front

insights.claim: Qatar reportedly tried to offer Iran covert support in exchange for guarantees against attacks on its LNG infrastructure, illustrating the GCC's lack of a unified front.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Individual Gulf states may cut side deals, complicating US-led security architecture.
insights.locator: However, the Gulf countries are not a unified front

insights.claim: Pipeline explosive attacks are usually repaired within hours or days, but pumping stations, offshore loading terminals and gas-oil separation plants can take months because of specialized equipment and recertification.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Outage duration depends on which node is hit; pumping stations and LNG trains are the long-tail risks.
insights.locator: Crews normally address individual explosive attacks

insights.claim: Excess processing capacity and alternative pipeline and export routes, as implemented in Saudi Arabia, can mitigate much of an attack's harm by preventing network stress.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Saudi redundancy makes its supply more resilient than peers.
insights.locator: However, large infrastructure with easily implementable

insights.claim: The authors warn that if interception cost ratios keep favoring attackers, Gulf states and the US may spend heavily for limited results, so they urge lower-cost low-altitude defenses plus spare parts inventories and rapid-repair capacity.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports demand for cheap counter-drone systems, interceptor restocking and energy-asset security services.
insights.quote: if the cost ratios continue to favor the aggressor, then the Gulf states and the United States may spend heavily to achieve only limited results

insights.claim: Iran's demonstrated ability to cripple Gulf output may push some Gulf states toward more pro-Tehran positions, new rules of engagement with red lines on energy infrastructure, or demands for more US security assistance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Could weaken Gulf-Israel normalization and US basing cooperation.

insights.claim: Iranian attacks on Western-linked assets could raise costs for Chevron, Exxon, Shell and other Western firms relative to non-Western competitors and lead Gulf governments to discourage US involvement in projects.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Western majors may lose Gulf project share to Asian national oil companies.

insights.claim: The threat of Iranian cells inside Gulf states may intensify internal security efforts and could lead to broader crackdowns on dissent.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rising domestic securitization in the Gulf has governance and stability implications.
